sections.learning_objective: Connect ACID properties to real failures.
sections.markdown: A transaction groups operations into one unit. Atomicity means all changes commit or none do. Consistency means constraints and application invariants hold at transaction boundaries. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe. Durability means a committed change survives a crash according to the database's persistence guarantees. ACID is behavior to design for, not merely vocabulary.
sections.title: ACID as observable guarantees

sections.markdown: `BEGIN` opens an explicit transaction, `COMMIT` makes its changes durable and visible, and `ROLLBACK` discards uncommitted changes. Keep boundaries around one business operation. If the credit update fails after the debit, roll back both. Long transactions retain locks or old row versions and increase contention.
sections.title: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK

sections.markdown: Transactions work with constraints, not instead of them. A check such as `balance >= 0`, a unique idempotency key, and foreign keys reject invalid intermediate results at the appropriate time. Application pre-checks alone have race windows: another transaction can change the data between the check and the write.
sections.title: Consistency through constraints

sections.learning_objective: Identify anomalies caused by overlapping work.
sections.markdown: Concurrent operations can cause dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom rows, or lost updates depending on the database and isolation level. PostgreSQL prevents dirty reads, but read-modify-write application code can still lose an update. Prefer an atomic update, or lock the selected row with `FOR UPDATE` when later decisions depend on it.
sections.title: Concurrency problems

sections.learning_objective: Choose isolation based on required invariants.
sections.markdown: Read Committed is PostgreSQL's default and each statement sees a fresh committed snapshot. Repeatable Read gives the transaction a stable snapshot. Serializable aims to produce a result equivalent to some serial execution, but may abort one transaction with a serialization failure. Robust applications use short transactions and retry the complete operation when the database reports a retryable conflict.
